AGRIPPA

1157Indeed, he plied them both with excellent praises.

ENOBARBUS

1158But he loves Caesar best, yet he loves Antony.
1159Hoo, hearts, tongues, figures, scribes, bards, poets, cannot
1160Think, speak, cast, write, sing, number—hoo!—
1161His love to Antony. But as for Caesar,
1162Kneel down, kneel down, and wonder.

AGRIPPA

Kneel down, kneel down, and wonder. Both he loves.

ENOBARBUS

1163They are his shards and he their beetle.

Trumpet within.

They are his shards and he their beetle. So,
1164This is to horse. Adieu, noble Agrippa.

AGRIPPA

1165Good fortune, worthy soldier, and farewell.

Enter Caesar, Antony, Lepidus, and Octavia.

ANTONY

Good fortune, worthy soldier, and farewell. No further, sir.

CAESAR

1166You take from me a great part of myself.
1167Use me well in ’t.—Sister, prove such a wife
1168As my thoughts make thee, and as my farthest bond
1169Shall pass on thy approof.—Most noble Antony,
1170Let not the piece of virtue which is set
1171Betwixt us, as the cement of our love
1172To keep it builded, be the ram to batter
1173The fortress of it. For better might we
1174Have loved without this mean, if on both parts
1175This be not cherished.

ANTONY

This be not cherished. Make me not offended
1176In your distrust.

CAESAR

In your distrust. I have said.

ANTONY

In your distrust. I have said. You shall not find,
1177Though you be therein curious, the least cause
1178For what you seem to fear. So the gods keep you,
1179And make the hearts of Romans serve your ends.
1180We will here part.

CAESAR

1181Farewell, my dearest sister, fare thee well.
1182The elements be kind to thee and make
1183Thy spirits all of comfort. Fare thee well.

OCTAVIA

1184My noble brother.

She weeps.

ANTONY

1185The April’s in her eyes. It is love’s spring,
1186And these the showers to bring it on.—Be cheerful.

OCTAVIA

1187To Caesar. Sir, look well to my husband’s house, and—

CAESAR

1188What, Octavia?

OCTAVIA

What, Octavia? I’ll tell you in your ear.

Caesar and Octavia walk aside.

ANTONY

1189Her tongue will not obey her heart, nor can
1190Her heart inform her tongue—the swan’s-down feather
1191That stands upon the swell at the full of tide
1192And neither way inclines.

ENOBARBUS

And neither way inclines. Aside to Agrippa. Will Caesar weep?aparte

AGRIPPA

1193He has a cloud in ’s face.

ENOBARBUS

1194He were the worse for that were he a horse;
1195So is he being a man.

AGRIPPA

So is he being a man. Why, Enobarbus,
1196When Antony found Julius Caesar dead,
1197He cried almost to roaring. And he wept
1198When at Philippi he found Brutus slain.

ENOBARBUS

1199That year indeed he was troubled with a rheum.
1200What willingly he did confound he wailed,
1201Believe ’t, till I wept too.

CAESAR

Believe ’t, till I wept too. Coming forward with Octavia. No, sweet Octavia,
1202You shall hear from me still. The time shall not
1203Outgo my thinking on you.

ANTONY

Outgo my thinking on you. Come, sir, come,
1204I’ll wrestle with you in my strength of love.
1205Look, here I have you, thus I let you go,
1206And give you to the gods.

CAESAR

And give you to the gods. Adieu, be happy.

LEPIDUS

1207To Antony. Let all the number of the stars give light
1208To thy fair way.

CAESAR

To thy fair way. Farewell, farewell.

Kisses Octavia.

ANTONY

To thy fair way. Farewell, farewell. Farewell.

Trumpets sound. They exit.

Scene 3

Enter Cleopatra, Charmian, Iras, and Alexas.

CLEOPATRA

1209Where is the fellow?

ALEXAS

Where is the fellow? Half afeard to come.

CLEOPATRA

1210Go to, go to.—Come hither, sir.

Enter the Messenger as before.

ALEXAS

Go to, go to.—Come hither, sir. Good Majesty,
1211Herod of Jewry dare not look upon you
1212But when you are well pleased.

CLEOPATRA

But when you are well pleased. That Herod’s head
1213I’ll have! But how, when Antony is gone,
1214Through whom I might command it?—Come thou near.

MESSENGER

1215Most gracious Majesty!

CLEOPATRA

Most gracious Majesty! Did’st thou behold Octavia?

MESSENGER

1216Ay, dread queen.

CLEOPATRA

Ay, dread queen. Where?

MESSENGER

Ay, dread queen. Where? Madam, in Rome.
1217I looked her in the face and saw her led
1218Between her brother and Mark Antony.

CLEOPATRA

1219Is she as tall as me?

MESSENGER

Is she as tall as me? She is not, madam.

CLEOPATRA

1220Didst hear her speak? Is she shrill-tongued or low?

MESSENGER

1221Madam, I heard her speak. She is low-voiced.

CLEOPATRA

1222That’s not so good. He cannot like her long.

CHARMIAN

1223Like her? O Isis, ’tis impossible!

CLEOPATRA

1224I think so, Charmian: dull of tongue, and dwarfish!—
1225What majesty is in her gait? Remember,
1226If e’er thou looked’st on majesty.

MESSENGER

If e’er thou looked’st on majesty. She creeps.
1227Her motion and her station are as one.
1228She shows a body rather than a life,
1229A statue than a breather.

CLEOPATRA

A statue than a breather. Is this certain?

MESSENGER

1230Or I have no observance.

CHARMIAN

Or I have no observance. Three in Egypt
1231Cannot make better note.

CLEOPATRA

Cannot make better note. He’s very knowing.
1232I do perceive ’t. There’s nothing in her yet.
1233The fellow has good judgment.

CHARMIAN

The fellow has good judgment. Excellent.

CLEOPATRA

1234To Messenger. Guess at her years, I prithee.

MESSENGER

1235Madam, she was a widow.

CLEOPATRA

1236Widow? Charmian, hark.

MESSENGER

1237And I do think she’s thirty.

CLEOPATRA

1238Bear’st thou her face in mind? Is ’t long or round?

MESSENGER

1239Round even to faultiness.

CLEOPATRA

1240For the most part, too, they are foolish that are so.
1241Her hair what color?

MESSENGER

1242Brown, madam, and her forehead
1243As low as she would wish it.

CLEOPATRA

As low as she would wish it. Giving money. There’s gold for thee.
1244Thou must not take my former sharpness ill.
1245I will employ thee back again. I find thee
1246Most fit for business. Go, make thee ready.
1247Our letters are prepared.

Messenger exits.

CHARMIAN

Our letters are prepared. A proper man.

CLEOPATRA

1248Indeed he is so. I repent me much
1249That so I harried him. Why, methinks, by him,
1250This creature’s no such thing.

CHARMIAN

This creature’s no such thing. Nothing, madam.

CLEOPATRA

1251The man hath seen some majesty, and should know.

CHARMIAN

1252Hath he seen majesty? Isis else defend,
1253And serving you so long!

CLEOPATRA

1254I have one thing more to ask him yet, good Charmian,
1255But ’tis no matter. Thou shalt bring him to me
1256Where I will write. All may be well enough.

CHARMIAN

1257I warrant you, madam.

They exit.

Scene 4

Enter Antony and Octavia.

ANTONY

1258Nay, nay, Octavia, not only that—
1259That were excusable, that and thousands more
1260Of semblable import—but he hath waged
1261New wars ’gainst Pompey; made his will and read it
1262To public ear;
1263Spoke scantly of me; when perforce he could not
1264But pay me terms of honor, cold and sickly
1265He vented them, most narrow measure lent me;
1266When the best hint was given him, he not took ’t,
1267Or did it from his teeth.

OCTAVIA

Or did it from his teeth. O, my good lord,
1268Believe not all, or if you must believe,
1269Stomach not all. A more unhappy lady,
1270If this division chance, ne’er stood between,
1271Praying for both parts.
1272The good gods will mock me presently
1273When I shall pray “O, bless my lord and husband!”
1274Undo that prayer by crying out as loud
1275“O, bless my brother!” Husband win, win brother
1276Prays and destroys the prayer; no midway
1277’Twixt these extremes at all.

ANTONY

’Twixt these extremes at all. Gentle Octavia,
1278Let your best love draw to that point which seeks
1279Best to preserve it. If I lose mine honor,
1280I lose myself; better I were not yours
1281Than yours so branchless. But, as you requested,
1282Yourself shall go between ’s. The meantime, lady,
1283I’ll raise the preparation of a war
1284Shall stain your brother. Make your soonest haste,
1285So your desires are yours.

OCTAVIA

So your desires are yours. Thanks to my lord.
1286The Jove of power make me, most weak, most weak,
1287Your reconciler. Wars ’twixt you twain would be
1288As if the world should cleave, and that slain men
1289Should solder up the rift.

ANTONY

1290When it appears to you where this begins,
1291Turn your displeasure that way, for our faults
1292Can never be so equal that your love
1293Can equally move with them. Provide your going;
1294Choose your own company, and command what cost
1295Your heart has mind to.

They exit.

Scene 5

Enter Enobarbus and Eros.

ENOBARBUS

1296How now, friend Eros?

EROS

1297There’s strange news come, sir.

ENOBARBUS

1298What, man?

EROS

1299Caesar and Lepidus have made wars upon Pompey.

ENOBARBUS

1300This is old. What is the success?

EROS

1301Caesar, having made use of him in the wars ’gainst Pompey, presently denied him rivality, would not let him partake in the glory of the action; and, not resting here, accuses him of letters he had formerly wrote to Pompey; upon his own appeal seizes him. So the poor third is up, till death enlarge his confine.

ENOBARBUS

1302Then, world, thou hast a pair of chaps, no more,
1303And throw between them all the food thou hast,
1304They’ll grind the one the other. Where’s Antony?

EROS

1305He’s walking in the garden, thus, and spurns
1306The rush that lies before him; cries “Fool Lepidus!”
1307And threats the throat of that his officer
1308That murdered Pompey.

ENOBARBUS

That murdered Pompey. Our great navy’s rigged.

EROS

1309For Italy and Caesar. More, Domitius:
1310My lord desires you presently. My news
1311I might have told hereafter.

ENOBARBUS

I might have told hereafter. ’Twill be naught,
1312But let it be. Bring me to Antony.

EROS

1313Come, sir.

They exit.

Scene 6

Enter Agrippa, Maecenas, and Caesar.

CAESAR

1314Contemning Rome, he has done all this and more
1315In Alexandria. Here’s the manner of ’t:
1316I’ th’ marketplace, on a tribunal silvered,
1317Cleopatra and himself in chairs of gold
1318Were publicly enthroned. At the feet sat
1319Caesarion, whom they call my father’s son,
1320And all the unlawful issue that their lust
1321Since then hath made between them. Unto her
1322He gave the stablishment of Egypt, made her
1323Of lower Syria, Cyprus, Lydia,
1324Absolute queen.

MAECENAS

Absolute queen. This in the public eye?

CAESAR

1325I’ th’ common showplace where they exercise.
1326His sons he there proclaimed the kings of kings.
1327Great Media, Parthia, and Armenia
1328He gave to Alexander; to Ptolemy he assigned
1329Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia. She
1330In th’ habiliments of the goddess Isis
1331That day appeared, and oft before gave audience,
1332As ’tis reported, so.

MAECENAS

As ’tis reported, so. Let Rome be thus informed.

AGRIPPA

1333Who, queasy with his insolence already,
1334Will their good thoughts call from him.

CAESAR

1335The people knows it and have now received
1336His accusations.

AGRIPPA

His accusations. Who does he accuse?

CAESAR

1337Caesar, and that, having in Sicily
1338Sextus Pompeius spoiled, we had not rated him
1339His part o’ th’ isle. Then does he say he lent me
1340Some shipping, unrestored. Lastly, he frets
1341That Lepidus of the triumvirate
1342Should be deposed and, being, that we detain
1343All his revenue.

AGRIPPA

All his revenue. Sir, this should be answered.

CAESAR

1344’Tis done already, and the messenger gone.
1345I have told him Lepidus was grown too cruel,
1346That he his high authority abused
1347And did deserve his change. For what I have conquered,
1348I grant him part; but then in his Armenia
1349And other of his conquered kingdoms I
1350Demand the like.

MAECENAS

Demand the like. He’ll never yield to that.

CAESAR

1351Nor must not then be yielded to in this.

Enter Octavia with her Train.

OCTAVIA

1352Hail, Caesar, and my lord! Hail, most dear Caesar.

CAESAR

1353That ever I should call thee castaway!

OCTAVIA

1354You have not called me so, nor have you cause.

CAESAR

1355Why have you stol’n upon us thus? You come not
1356Like Caesar’s sister. The wife of Antony
1357Should have an army for an usher and
1358The neighs of horse to tell of her approach
1359Long ere she did appear. The trees by th’ way
1360Should have borne men, and expectation fainted,
1361Longing for what it had not. Nay, the dust
1362Should have ascended to the roof of heaven,
1363Raised by your populous troops. But you are come
1364A market-maid to Rome, and have prevented
1365The ostentation of our love, which, left unshown,
1366Is often left unloved. We should have met you
1367By sea and land, supplying every stage
1368With an augmented greeting.

OCTAVIA

With an augmented greeting. Good my lord,
1369To come thus was I not constrained, but did it
1370On my free will. My lord, Mark Antony,
1371Hearing that you prepared for war, acquainted
1372My grievèd ear withal, whereon I begged
1373His pardon for return.

CAESAR

His pardon for return. Which soon he granted,
1374Being an abstract ’tween his lust and him.

OCTAVIA

1375Do not say so, my lord.

CAESAR

Do not say so, my lord. I have eyes upon him,
1376And his affairs come to me on the wind.
1377Where is he now?

OCTAVIA

Where is he now? My lord, in Athens.

CAESAR

1378No, my most wrongèd sister. Cleopatra
1379Hath nodded him to her. He hath given his empire
1380Up to a whore, who now are levying
1381The kings o’ th’ Earth for war. He hath assembled
1382Bocchus, the King of Libya; Archelaus
1383Of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, King
1384Of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king, Adallas;
1385King Manchus of Arabia; King of Pont;
1386Herod of Jewry; Mithridates, King
1387Of Comagen; Polemon and Amyntas,
1388The Kings of Mede and Lycaonia,
1389With a more larger list of scepters.

OCTAVIA

1390Ay me, most wretched,
1391That have my heart parted betwixt two friends
1392That does afflict each other!

CAESAR

That does afflict each other! Welcome hither.
1393Your letters did withhold our breaking forth
1394Till we perceived both how you were wrong led
1395And we in negligent danger. Cheer your heart.
1396Be you not troubled with the time, which drives
1397O’er your content these strong necessities,
1398But let determined things to destiny
1399Hold unbewailed their way. Welcome to Rome,
1400Nothing more dear to me. You are abused
1401Beyond the mark of thought, and the high gods,
1402To do you justice, makes his ministers
1403Of us and those that love you. Best of comfort,
1404And ever welcome to us.

AGRIPPA

And ever welcome to us. Welcome, lady.

MAECENAS

1405Welcome, dear madam.
1406Each heart in Rome does love and pity you;
1407Only th’ adulterous Antony, most large
1408In his abominations, turns you off
1409And gives his potent regiment to a trull
1410That noises it against us.

OCTAVIA

That noises it against us. To Caesar Is it so, sir?

CAESAR

1411Most certain. Sister, welcome. Pray you
1412Be ever known to patience. My dear’st sister!

They exit.

Scene 7

Enter Cleopatra and Enobarbus.

CLEOPATRA

1413I will be even with thee, doubt it not.

ENOBARBUS

1414But why, why, why?

CLEOPATRA

1415Thou hast forspoke my being in these wars
1416And say’st it is not fit.

ENOBARBUS

And say’st it is not fit. Well, is it, is it?

CLEOPATRA

1417Is ’t not denounced against us? Why should not we
1418Be there in person?

ENOBARBUS

Be there in person? Well, I could reply:
1419If we should serve with horse and mares together,
1420The horse were merely lost. The mares would bear
1421A soldier and his horse.

CLEOPATRA

A soldier and his horse. What is ’t you say?

ENOBARBUS

1422Your presence needs must puzzle Antony,
1423Take from his heart, take from his brain, from ’s time
1424What should not then be spared. He is already
1425Traduced for levity, and ’tis said in Rome
1426That Photinus, an eunuch, and your maids
1427Manage this war.

CLEOPATRA

Manage this war. Sink Rome, and their tongues rot
1428That speak against us! A charge we bear i’ th’ war,
1429And as the president of my kingdom will
1430Appear there for a man. Speak not against it.
1431I will not stay behind.

Enter Antony and Canidius.

ENOBARBUS

I will not stay behind. Nay, I have done.
1432Here comes the Emperor.

ANTONY

Here comes the Emperor. Is it not strange, Canidius,
1433That from Tarentum and Brundusium
1434He could so quickly cut the Ionian Sea
1435And take in Toryne?—You have heard on ’t, sweet?

CLEOPATRA

1436Celerity is never more admired
1437Than by the negligent.

ANTONY

Than by the negligent. A good rebuke,
1438Which might have well becomed the best of men,
1439To taunt at slackness.—Canidius, we will fight
1440With him by sea.

CLEOPATRA

With him by sea. By sea, what else?

CANIDIUS

With him by sea. By sea, what else? Why will
1441My lord do so?

ANTONY

My lord do so? For that he dares us to ’t.

ENOBARBUS

1442So hath my lord dared him to single fight.

CANIDIUS

1443Ay, and to wage this battle at Pharsalia,
1444Where Caesar fought with Pompey. But these offers,
1445Which serve not for his vantage, he shakes off,
1446And so should you.

ENOBARBUS

And so should you. Your ships are not well manned,
1447Your mariners are muleteers, reapers, people
1448Engrossed by swift impress. In Caesar’s fleet
1449Are those that often have ’gainst Pompey fought.
1450Their ships are yare, yours heavy. No disgrace
1451Shall fall you for refusing him at sea,
1452Being prepared for land.

ANTONY

Being prepared for land. By sea, by sea.

ENOBARBUS

1453Most worthy sir, you therein throw away
1454The absolute soldiership you have by land,
1455Distract your army, which doth most consist
1456Of war-marked footmen, leave unexecuted
1457Your own renownèd knowledge, quite forgo
1458The way which promises assurance, and
1459Give up yourself merely to chance and hazard
1460From firm security.

ANTONY

From firm security. I’ll fight at sea.

CLEOPATRA

1461I have sixty sails, Caesar none better.

ANTONY

1462Our overplus of shipping will we burn,
1463And with the rest full-manned, from th’ head of Actium
1464Beat th’ approaching Caesar. But if we fail,
1465We then can do ’t at land.

Enter a Messenger.

We then can do ’t at land. Thy business?

MESSENGER

1466The news is true, my lord; he is descried.
1467Caesar has taken Toryne.

He exits.

ANTONY

1468Can he be there in person? ’Tis impossible;
1469Strange that his power should be. Canidius,
1470Our nineteen legions thou shalt hold by land,
1471And our twelve thousand horse. We’ll to our ship.—
1472Away, my Thetis.

Enter a Soldier.

Away, my Thetis. How now, worthy soldier?

SOLDIER

1473O noble emperor, do not fight by sea!
1474Trust not to rotten planks. Do you misdoubt
1475This sword and these my wounds? Let th’ Egyptians
1476And the Phoenicians go a-ducking. We
1477Have used to conquer standing on the earth
1478And fighting foot to foot.

ANTONY

And fighting foot to foot. Well, well, away.

Antony, Cleopatra, and Enobarbus exit.

SOLDIER

1479By Hercules, I think I am i’ th’ right.

CANIDIUS

1480Soldier, thou art, but his whole action grows
1481Not in the power on ’t. So our leader’s led,
1482And we are women’s men.

SOLDIER

And we are women’s men. You keep by land
1483The legions and the horse whole, do you not?

CANIDIUS

1484Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius,
1485Publicola, and Caelius are for sea,
1486But we keep whole by land. This speed of Caesar’s
1487Carries beyond belief.

SOLDIER

Carries beyond belief. While he was yet in Rome,
1488His power went out in such distractions as
1489Beguiled all spies.

CANIDIUS

Beguiled all spies. Who’s his lieutenant, hear you?

SOLDIER

1490They say one Taurus.

CANIDIUS

They say one Taurus. Well I know the man.

Enter a Messenger.

MESSENGER

1491The Emperor calls Canidius.

CANIDIUS

1492With news the time’s in labor, and throws forth
1493Each minute some.

They exit.

Scene 8

Enter Caesar with his army, and Taurus, marching.

CAESAR

1494Taurus!

TAURUS

1495My lord?

CAESAR

1496Strike not by land, keep whole. Provoke not battle
1497Till we have done at sea. Do not exceed
1498The prescript of this scroll.

Hands him a scroll.

The prescript of this scroll. Our fortune lies
1499Upon this jump.

They exit.

Scene 9

Enter Antony and Enobarbus.

ANTONY

1500Set we our squadrons on yond side o’ th’ hill
1501In eye of Caesar’s battle, from which place
1502We may the number of the ships behold
1503And so proceed accordingly.

They exit.

Scene 10

Canidius marcheth with his land army one way over the stage, and Taurus the lieutenant of Caesar the other way. After their going in is heard the noise of a sea fight.

Alarum. Enter Enobarbus.

ENOBARBUS

1504Naught, naught, all naught! I can behold no longer.
1505Th’ Antoniad, the Egyptian admiral,
1506With all their sixty, fly and turn the rudder.
1507To see ’t mine eyes are blasted.

Enter Scarus.

SCARUS

To see ’t mine eyes are blasted. Gods and goddesses,
1508All the whole synod of them!

ENOBARBUS

All the whole synod of them! What’s thy passion?

SCARUS

1509The greater cantle of the world is lost
1510With very ignorance. We have kissed away
1511Kingdoms and provinces.

ENOBARBUS

Kingdoms and provinces. How appears the fight?

SCARUS

1512On our side, like the tokened pestilence,
1513Where death is sure. Yon ribaudred nag of Egypt,
1514Whom leprosy o’ertake, i’ th’ midst o’ th’ fight,
1515When vantage like a pair of twins appeared
1516Both as the same—or, rather, ours the elder—
1517The breeze upon her like a cow in June,
1518Hoists sails and flies.

ENOBARBUS

Hoists sails and flies. That I beheld.
1519Mine eyes did sicken at the sight and could not
1520Endure a further view.

SCARUS

Endure a further view. She once being loofed,
1521The noble ruin of her magic, Antony,
1522Claps on his sea-wing and, like a doting mallard,
1523Leaving the fight in height, flies after her.
1524I never saw an action of such shame.
1525Experience, manhood, honor ne’er before
1526Did violate so itself.

ENOBARBUS

Did violate so itself. Alack, alack.

Enter Canidius.

CANIDIUS

1527Our fortune on the sea is out of breath
1528And sinks most lamentably. Had our general
1529Been what he knew himself, it had gone well.
1530O, he has given example for our flight
1531Most grossly by his own.

ENOBARBUS

1532Ay, are you thereabouts? Why then goodnight indeed.

CANIDIUS

1533Toward Peloponnesus are they fled.

SCARUS

1534’Tis easy to ’t, and there I will attend
1535What further comes.

He exits.

CANIDIUS

What further comes. To Caesar will I render
1536My legions and my horse. Six kings already
1537Show me the way of yielding.

He exits.

ENOBARBUS

Show me the way of yielding. I’ll yet follow
1538The wounded chance of Antony, though my reason
1539Sits in the wind against me.

He exits.

Scene 11

Enter Antony with Attendants.

ANTONY

1540Hark, the land bids me tread no more upon ’t.
1541It is ashamed to bear me. Friends, come hither.
1542I am so lated in the world that I
1543Have lost my way forever. I have a ship
1544Laden with gold. Take that, divide it. Fly,
1545And make your peace with Caesar.

ALL

And make your peace with Caesar. Fly? Not we!

ANTONY

1546I have fled myself and have instructed cowards
1547To run and show their shoulders. Friends, begone.
1548I have myself resolved upon a course
1549Which has no need of you. Begone.
1550My treasure’s in the harbor; take it. O,
1551I followed that I blush to look upon!
1552My very hairs do mutiny, for the white
1553Reprove the brown for rashness, and they them
1554For fear and doting. Friends, begone. You shall
1555Have letters from me to some friends that will
1556Sweep your way for you. Pray you look not sad,
1557Nor make replies of loathness. Take the hint
1558Which my despair proclaims. Let that be left
1559Which leaves itself. To the seaside straightway!
1560I will possess you of that ship and treasure.
1561Leave me, I pray, a little—pray you, now,
1562Nay, do so—for indeed I have lost command.
1563Therefore I pray you—I’ll see you by and by.

Attendants move aside. Antony sits down.

Enter Cleopatra led by Charmian, Iras, and Eros.

2377Give me some wine, and let me speak a little.

CLEOPATRA

2378No, let me speak, and let me rail so high
2379That the false huswife Fortune break her wheel,
2380Provoked by my offense.

ANTONY

Provoked by my offense. One word, sweet queen:
2381Of Caesar seek your honor with your safety—O!

CLEOPATRA

2382They do not go together.

ANTONY

They do not go together. Gentle, hear me.
2383None about Caesar trust but Proculeius.

CLEOPATRA

2384My resolution and my hands I’ll trust,
2385None about Caesar.

ANTONY

2386The miserable change now at my end
2387Lament nor sorrow at, but please your thoughts
2388In feeding them with those my former fortunes
2389Wherein I lived the greatest prince o’ th’ world,
2390The noblest, and do now not basely die,
2391Not cowardly put off my helmet to
2392My countryman—a Roman by a Roman
2393Valiantly vanquished. Now my spirit is going;
2394I can no more.

CLEOPATRA

I can no more. Noblest of men, woo’t die?
2395Hast thou no care of me? Shall I abide
2396In this dull world, which in thy absence is
2397No better than a sty? O see, my women,
2398The crown o’ th’ Earth doth melt.—My lord!

Antony dies.

2399O, withered is the garland of the war;
2400The soldier’s pole is fall’n; young boys and girls
2401Are level now with men. The odds is gone,
2402And there is nothing left remarkable
2403Beneath the visiting moon.

CHARMIAN

Beneath the visiting moon. O, quietness, lady!

Cleopatra swoons.

IRAS

2404She’s dead, too, our sovereign.

CHARMIAN

2405Lady!

IRAS

2406Madam!

CHARMIAN

2407O madam, madam, madam!

IRAS

2408Royal Egypt! Empress!

Cleopatra stirs.

CHARMIAN

2409Peace, peace, Iras!

CLEOPATRA

2410No more but e’en a woman, and commanded
2411By such poor passion as the maid that milks
2412And does the meanest chares. It were for me
2413To throw my scepter at the injurious gods,
2414To tell them that this world did equal theirs
2415Till they had stolen our jewel. All’s but naught.
2416Patience is sottish, and impatience does
2417Become a dog that’s mad. Then is it sin
2418To rush into the secret house of death
2419Ere death dare come to us? How do you, women?
2420What, what, good cheer! Why, how now, Charmian?
2421My noble girls! Ah, women, women! Look,
2422Our lamp is spent; it’s out. Good sirs, take heart.
2423We’ll bury him; and then, what’s brave, what’s noble,
2424Let’s do ’t after the high Roman fashion
2425And make death proud to take us. Come, away.
2426This case of that huge spirit now is cold.
2427Ah women, women! Come, we have no friend
2428But resolution and the briefest end.

They exit, bearing off Antony’s body.

Act V

Scene 1

Enter Caesar with Agrippa, Dolabella, Maecenas, Gallus, and Proculeius, his council of war.

CAESAR

2429Aside to Dolabella. Go to him, Dolabella, bid him yield.aparte
2430Being so frustrate, tell him, he mocks
2431The pauses that he makes.

DOLABELLA

The pauses that he makes. Caesar, I shall.

Dolabella exits.

Enter Dercetus with the sword of Antony.

CAESAR

2432Wherefore is that? And what art thou that dar’st
2433Appear thus to us?

DERCETUS

Appear thus to us? I am called Dercetus.
2434Mark Antony I served, who best was worthy
2435Best to be served. Whilst he stood up and spoke,
2436He was my master, and I wore my life
2437To spend upon his haters. If thou please
2438To take me to thee, as I was to him
2439I’ll be to Caesar; if thou pleasest not,
2440I yield thee up my life.

CAESAR

I yield thee up my life. What is ’t thou say’st?

DERCETUS

2441I say, O Caesar, Antony is dead.

CAESAR

2442The breaking of so great a thing should make
2443A greater crack. The round world
2444Should have shook lions into civil streets
2445And citizens to their dens. The death of Antony
2446Is not a single doom; in the name lay
2447A moiety of the world.

DERCETUS

A moiety of the world. He is dead, Caesar,
2448Not by a public minister of justice,
2449Nor by a hirèd knife, but that self hand
2450Which writ his honor in the acts it did
2451Hath, with the courage which the heart did lend it,
2452Splitted the heart. This is his sword.
2453I robbed his wound of it. Behold it stained
2454With his most noble blood.

CAESAR

With his most noble blood. Look you sad, friends?
2455The gods rebuke me, but it is tidings
2456To wash the eyes of kings.

AGRIPPA

To wash the eyes of kings. And strange it is
2457That nature must compel us to lament
2458Our most persisted deeds.

MAECENAS

Our most persisted deeds. His taints and honors
2459Waged equal with him.

AGRIPPA

Waged equal with him. A rarer spirit never
2460Did steer humanity, but you gods will give us
2461Some faults to make us men. Caesar is touched.

MAECENAS

2462When such a spacious mirror’s set before him,
2463He needs must see himself.

CAESAR

He needs must see himself. O Antony,
2464I have followed thee to this, but we do lance
2465Diseases in our bodies. I must perforce
2466Have shown to thee such a declining day
2467Or look on thine. We could not stall together
2468In the whole world. But yet let me lament
2469With tears as sovereign as the blood of hearts
2470That thou my brother, my competitor
2471In top of all design, my mate in empire,
2472Friend and companion in the front of war,
2473The arm of mine own body, and the heart
2474Where mine his thoughts did kindle—that our stars
2475Unreconciliable should divide
2476Our equalness to this. Hear me, good friends—

Enter an Egyptian.

2477But I will tell you at some meeter season.
2478The business of this man looks out of him.
2479We’ll hear him what he says.—Whence are you?

EGYPTIAN

2480A poor Egyptian yet, the Queen my mistress,
2481Confined in all she has, her monument,
2482Of thy intents desires instruction,
2483That she preparedly may frame herself
2484To th’ way she’s forced to.

CAESAR

To th’ way she’s forced to. Bid her have good heart.
2485She soon shall know of us, by some of ours,
2486How honorable and how kindly we
2487Determine for her. For Caesar cannot live
2488To be ungentle.

EGYPTIAN

To be ungentle. So the gods preserve thee.

He exits.

CAESAR

2489Come hither, Proculeius. Go and say
2490We purpose her no shame. Give her what comforts
2491The quality of her passion shall require,
2492Lest, in her greatness, by some mortal stroke
2493She do defeat us, for her life in Rome
2494Would be eternal in our triumph. Go,
2495And with your speediest bring us what she says
2496And how you find of her.

PROCULEIUS

And how you find of her. Caesar, I shall.

Proculeius exits.

CAESAR

2497Gallus, go you along.

Gallus exits.

Gallus, go you along. Where’s Dolabella,
2498To second Proculeius?

ALL

To second Proculeius? Dollabella!

CAESAR

2499Let him alone, for I remember now
2500How he’s employed. He shall in time be ready.
2501Go with me to my tent, where you shall see
2502How hardly I was drawn into this war,
2503How calm and gentle I proceeded still
2504In all my writings. Go with me and see
2505What I can show in this.

They exit.

Scene 2

Enter Cleopatra, Charmian, and Iras.

CLEOPATRA

2506My desolation does begin to make
2507A better life. ’Tis paltry to be Caesar;
2508Not being Fortune, he’s but Fortune’s knave,
2509A minister of her will. And it is great
2510To do that thing that ends all other deeds,
2511Which shackles accidents and bolts up change,
2512Which sleeps and never palates more the dung,
2513The beggar’s nurse, and Caesar’s.

Enter Proculeius.

PROCULEIUS

2514Caesar sends greeting to the Queen of Egypt,
2515And bids thee study on what fair demands
2516Thou mean’st to have him grant thee.

CLEOPATRA

Thou mean’st to have him grant thee. What’s thy name?

PROCULEIUS

2517My name is Proculeius.

CLEOPATRA

My name is Proculeius. Antony
2518Did tell me of you, bade me trust you, but
2519I do not greatly care to be deceived
2520That have no use for trusting. If your master
2521Would have a queen his beggar, you must tell him
2522That majesty, to keep decorum, must
2523No less beg than a kingdom. If he please
2524To give me conquered Egypt for my son,
2525He gives me so much of mine own as I
2526Will kneel to him with thanks.

PROCULEIUS

Will kneel to him with thanks. Be of good cheer.
2527You’re fall’n into a princely hand; fear nothing.
2528Make your full reference freely to my lord,
2529Who is so full of grace that it flows over
2530On all that need. Let me report to him
2531Your sweet dependency, and you shall find
2532A conqueror that will pray in aid for kindness
2533Where he for grace is kneeled to.

CLEOPATRA

Where he for grace is kneeled to. Pray you tell him
2534I am his fortune’s vassal and I send him
2535The greatness he has got. I hourly learn
2536A doctrine of obedience, and would gladly
2537Look him i’ th’ face.

PROCULEIUS

Look him i’ th’ face. This I’ll report, dear lady.
2538Have comfort, for I know your plight is pitied
2539Of him that caused it.

GALLUS

2540You see how easily she may be surprised.
2541Guard her till Caesar come.

IRAS

Guard her till Caesar come. Royal queen!

CHARMIAN

2542O, Cleopatra, thou art taken, queen!

CLEOPATRA

2543Drawing a dagger. Quick, quick, good hands!

PROCULEIUS

2544Seizing the dagger. Hold, worthy lady, hold!
2545Do not yourself such wrong, who are in this
2546Relieved, but not betrayed.

CLEOPATRA

Relieved, but not betrayed. What, of death, too,
2547That rids our dogs of languish?

PROCULEIUS

That rids our dogs of languish? Cleopatra,
2548Do not abuse my master’s bounty by
2549Th’ undoing of yourself. Let the world see
2550His nobleness well acted, which your death
2551Will never let come forth.

CLEOPATRA

Will never let come forth. Where art thou, Death?
2552Come hither, come! Come, come, and take a queen
2553Worth many babes and beggars.

PROCULEIUS

Worth many babes and beggars. O, temperance, lady!

CLEOPATRA

2554Sir, I will eat no meat; I’ll not drink, sir.
2555If idle talk will once be necessary—
2556I’ll not sleep neither. This mortal house I’ll ruin,
2557Do Caesar what he can. Know, sir, that I
2558Will not wait pinioned at your master’s court,
2559Nor once be chastised with the sober eye
2560Of dull Octavia. Shall they hoist me up
2561And show me to the shouting varletry
2562Of censuring Rome? Rather a ditch in Egypt
2563Be gentle grave unto me; rather on Nilus’ mud
2564Lay me stark naked, and let the waterflies
2565Blow me into abhorring; rather make
2566My country’s high pyramides my gibbet
2567And hang me up in chains!

PROCULEIUS

And hang me up in chains! You do extend
2568These thoughts of horror further than you shall
2569Find cause in Caesar.

Enter Dolabella.

DOLABELLA

Find cause in Caesar. Proculeius,
2570What thou hast done thy master Caesar knows,
2571And he hath sent for thee. For the Queen,
2572I’ll take her to my guard.

PROCULEIUS

I’ll take her to my guard. So, Dolabella,
2573It shall content me best. Be gentle to her.
2574To Cleopatra. To Caesar I will speak what you shall please,
2575If you’ll employ me to him.

CLEOPATRA

If you’ll employ me to him. Say I would die.

Proculeius, Gallus, and Soldiers exit.

DOLABELLA

2576Most noble empress, you have heard of me.

CLEOPATRA

2577I cannot tell.

DOLABELLA

I cannot tell. Assuredly you know me.

CLEOPATRA

2578No matter, sir, what I have heard or known.
2579You laugh when boys or women tell their dreams;
2580Is ’t not your trick?

DOLABELLA

Is ’t not your trick? I understand not, madam.

CLEOPATRA

2581I dreamt there was an emperor Antony.
2582O, such another sleep, that I might see
2583But such another man.

DOLABELLA

But such another man. If it might please you—

CLEOPATRA

2584His face was as the heavens, and therein stuck
2585A sun and moon, which kept their course and lighted
2586The little O, the Earth.

DOLABELLA

The little O, the Earth. Most sovereign creature—

CLEOPATRA

2587His legs bestrid the ocean, his reared arm
2588Crested the world. His voice was propertied
2589As all the tunèd spheres, and that to friends;
2590But when he meant to quail and shake the orb,
2591He was as rattling thunder. For his bounty,
2592There was no winter in ’t; an autumn ’twas
2593That grew the more by reaping. His delights
2594Were dolphin-like; they showed his back above
2595The element they lived in. In his livery
2596Walked crowns and crownets; realms and islands were
2597As plates dropped from his pocket.

DOLABELLA

As plates dropped from his pocket. Cleopatra—

CLEOPATRA

2598Think you there was, or might be, such a man
2599As this I dreamt of?

DOLABELLA

As this I dreamt of? Gentle madam, no.

CLEOPATRA

2600You lie up to the hearing of the gods!
2601But if there be nor ever were one such,
2602It’s past the size of dreaming. Nature wants stuff
2603To vie strange forms with fancy, yet t’ imagine
2604An Antony were nature’s piece ’gainst fancy,
2605Condemning shadows quite.

DOLABELLA

Condemning shadows quite. Hear me, good madam.
2606Your loss is as yourself, great; and you bear it
2607As answering to the weight. Would I might never
2608O’ertake pursued success but I do feel,
2609By the rebound of yours, a grief that smites
2610My very heart at root.

CLEOPATRA

My very heart at root. I thank you, sir.
2611Know you what Caesar means to do with me?

DOLABELLA

2612I am loath to tell you what I would you knew.

CLEOPATRA

2613Nay, pray you, sir.

DOLABELLA

Nay, pray you, sir. Though he be honorable—

CLEOPATRA

2614He’ll lead me, then, in triumph.

DOLABELLA

2615Madam, he will. I know ’t.

Flourish. Enter Caesar, Proculeius, Gallus, Maecenas, and others of his train.

ALL

2616Make way there! Caesar!

CAESAR

2617Which is the Queen of Egypt?

DOLABELLA

2618It is the Emperor, madam.

Cleopatra kneels.

CAESAR

2619Arise. You shall not kneel.
2620I pray you, rise. Rise, Egypt.

CLEOPATRA

I pray you, rise. Rise, Egypt. Sir, the gods
2621Will have it thus. My master and my lord
2622I must obey.

She stands.

CAESAR

I must obey. Take to you no hard thoughts.
2623The record of what injuries you did us,
2624Though written in our flesh, we shall remember
2625As things but done by chance.

CLEOPATRA

As things but done by chance. Sole sir o’ th’ world,
2626I cannot project mine own cause so well
2627To make it clear, but do confess I have
2628Been laden with like frailties which before
2629Have often shamed our sex.

CAESAR

Have often shamed our sex. Cleopatra, know
2630We will extenuate rather than enforce.
2631If you apply yourself to our intents,
2632Which towards you are most gentle, you shall find
2633A benefit in this change; but if you seek
2634To lay on me a cruelty by taking
2635Antony’s course, you shall bereave yourself
2636Of my good purposes, and put your children
2637To that destruction which I’ll guard them from
2638If thereon you rely. I’ll take my leave.

CLEOPATRA

2639And may through all the world. ’Tis yours, and we,
2640Your scutcheons and your signs of conquest, shall
2641Hang in what place you please. Here, my good lord.

She holds out a paper.

CAESAR

2642You shall advise me in all for Cleopatra.

CLEOPATRA

2643This is the brief of money, plate, and jewels
2644I am possessed of. ’Tis exactly valued,
2645Not petty things admitted.—Where’s Seleucus?

Enter Seleucus.

SELEUCUS

2646Here, madam.

CLEOPATRA

2647This is my treasurer. Let him speak, my lord,
2648Upon his peril, that I have reserved
2649To myself nothing.—Speak the truth, Seleucus.

SELEUCUS

2650Madam, I had rather seel my lips
2651Than to my peril speak that which is not.

CLEOPATRA

2652What have I kept back?

SELEUCUS

2653Enough to purchase what you have made known.

CAESAR

2654Nay, blush not, Cleopatra. I approve
2655Your wisdom in the deed.

CLEOPATRA

Your wisdom in the deed. See, Caesar, O, behold
2656How pomp is followed! Mine will now be yours,
2657And should we shift estates, yours would be mine.
2658The ingratitude of this Seleucus does
2659Even make me wild.—O slave, of no more trust
2660Than love that’s hired! What, goest thou back? Thou shalt
2661Go back, I warrant thee! But I’ll catch thine eyes
2662Though they had wings. Slave, soulless villain, dog!
2663O rarely base!

CAESAR

O rarely base! Good queen, let us entreat you—

CLEOPATRA

2664O Caesar, what a wounding shame is this,
2665That thou vouchsafing here to visit me,
2666Doing the honor of thy lordliness
2667To one so meek, that mine own servant should
2668Parcel the sum of my disgraces by
2669Addition of his envy! Say, good Caesar,
2670That I some lady trifles have reserved,
2671Immoment toys, things of such dignity
2672As we greet modern friends withal, and say
2673Some nobler token I have kept apart
2674For Livia and Octavia, to induce
2675Their mediation, must I be unfolded
2676With one that I have bred? The gods! It smites me
2677Beneath the fall I have. To Seleucus. Prithee, go hence,
2678Or I shall show the cinders of my spirits
2679Through th’ ashes of my chance. Wert thou a man,
2680Thou wouldst have mercy on me.

CAESAR

Thou wouldst have mercy on me. Forbear, Seleucus.

Seleucus exits.

CLEOPATRA

2681Be it known that we, the greatest, are misthought
2682For things that others do; and when we fall,
2683We answer others’ merits in our name—
2684Are therefore to be pitied.

CAESAR

Are therefore to be pitied. Cleopatra,
2685Not what you have reserved nor what acknowledged
2686Put we i’ th’ roll of conquest. Still be ’t yours!
2687Bestow it at your pleasure, and believe
2688Caesar’s no merchant to make prize with you
2689Of things that merchants sold. Therefore be cheered.
2690Make not your thoughts your prisons. No, dear queen,
2691For we intend so to dispose you as
2692Yourself shall give us counsel. Feed and sleep.
2693Our care and pity is so much upon you
2694That we remain your friend. And so adieu.

CLEOPATRA

2695My master and my lord!

CAESAR

My master and my lord! Not so. Adieu.
2696Flourish. Caesar and his train exit.

CLEOPATRA

2697He words me, girls, he words me, that I should not
2698Be noble to myself. But hark thee, Charmian.

She whispers to Charmian.

IRAS

2699Finish, good lady. The bright day is done,
2700And we are for the dark.

CLEOPATRA

And we are for the dark. To Charmian. Hie thee again.
2701I have spoke already, and it is provided.
2702Go put it to the haste.

CHARMIAN

Go put it to the haste. Madam, I will.

Enter Dolabella.

DOLABELLA

2703Where’s the Queen?

CHARMIAN

Where’s the Queen? Behold, sir.

She exits.

CLEOPATRA

Where’s the Queen? Behold, sir. Dolabella.

DOLABELLA

2704Madam, as thereto sworn by your command,
2705Which my love makes religion to obey,
2706I tell you this: Caesar through Syria
2707Intends his journey, and within three days
2708You with your children will he send before.
2709Make your best use of this. I have performed
2710Your pleasure and my promise.

CLEOPATRA

Your pleasure and my promise. Dolabella,
2711I shall remain your debtor.

DOLABELLA

I shall remain your debtor. I your servant.
2712Adieu, good queen. I must attend on Caesar.

CLEOPATRA

2713Farewell, and thanks.

He exits.

Farewell, and thanks. Now, Iras, what think’st thou?
2714Thou an Egyptian puppet shall be shown
2715In Rome as well as I. Mechanic slaves
2716With greasy aprons, rules, and hammers shall
2717Uplift us to the view. In their thick breaths,
2718Rank of gross diet, shall we be enclouded
2719And forced to drink their vapor.

IRAS

And forced to drink their vapor. The gods forbid!

CLEOPATRA

2720Nay, ’tis most certain, Iras. Saucy lictors
2721Will catch at us like strumpets, and scald rhymers
2722Ballad us out o’ tune. The quick comedians
2723Extemporally will stage us and present
2724Our Alexandrian revels. Antony
2725Shall be brought drunken forth, and I shall see
2726Some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness
2727I’ th’ posture of a whore.

IRAS

I’ th’ posture of a whore. O the good gods!

CLEOPATRA

2728Nay, that’s certain.

IRAS

2729I’ll never see ’t! For I am sure mine nails
2730Are stronger than mine eyes.

CLEOPATRA

Are stronger than mine eyes. Why, that’s the way
2731To fool their preparation and to conquer
2732Their most absurd intents.

Enter Charmian.

Their most absurd intents. Now, Charmian!
2733Show me, my women, like a queen. Go fetch
2734My best attires. I am again for Cydnus
2735To meet Mark Antony. Sirrah Iras, go.—
2736Now, noble Charmian, we’ll dispatch indeed,
2737And when thou hast done this chare, I’ll give thee leave
2738To play till Doomsday.—Bring our crown and all.

Iras exits. A noise within.

2739Wherefore’s this noise?

Enter a Guardsman.

GUARDSMAN

Wherefore’s this noise? Here is a rural fellow
2740That will not be denied your Highness’ presence.
2741He brings you figs.

CLEOPATRA

2742Let him come in.

Guardsman exits.

Let him come in. What poor an instrument
2743May do a noble deed! He brings me liberty.
2744My resolution’s placed, and I have nothing
2745Of woman in me. Now from head to foot
2746I am marble-constant. Now the fleeting moon
2747No planet is of mine.

Enter Guardsman and Countryman, with a basket.

GUARDSMAN

No planet is of mine. This is the man.

CLEOPATRA

2748Avoid, and leave him.

Guardsman exits.

2749Hast thou the pretty worm of Nilus there
2750That kills and pains not?

COUNTRYMAN

Truly I have him, but I would not be the party that should desire you to touch him, for his biting is immortal. Those that do die of it do seldom or never recover.

CLEOPATRA

2751Remember’st thou any that have died on ’t?

COUNTRYMAN

Very many, men and women too. I heard of one of them no longer than yesterday—a very honest woman, but something given to lie, as a woman should not do but in the way of honesty—how she died of the biting of it, what pain she felt. Truly, she makes a very good report o’ th’ worm. But he that will believe all that they say shall never be saved by half that they do. But this is most falliable, the worm’s an odd worm.

CLEOPATRA

2752Get thee hence. Farewell.

COUNTRYMAN

I wish you all joy of the worm.

He sets down the basket.

CLEOPATRA

2753Farewell.

COUNTRYMAN

You must think this, look you, that the worm will do his kind.

CLEOPATRA

2754Ay, ay, farewell.

COUNTRYMAN

Look you, the worm is not to be trusted but in the keeping of wise people, for indeed there is no goodness in the worm.

CLEOPATRA

2755Take thou no care; it shall be heeded.

COUNTRYMAN

Very good. Give it nothing, I pray you, for it is not worth the feeding.

CLEOPATRA

2756Will it eat me?

COUNTRYMAN

You must not think I am so simple but I know the devil himself will not eat a woman. I know that a woman is a dish for the gods if the devil dress her not. But truly these same whoreson devils do the gods great harm in their women, for in every ten that they make, the devils mar five.

CLEOPATRA

2757Well, get thee gone. Farewell.

COUNTRYMAN

Yes, forsooth. I wish you joy o’ th’ worm.

He exits.

Enter Iras bearing Cleopatra’s royal regalia.

CLEOPATRA

2758Give me my robe. Put on my crown. I have
2759Immortal longings in me. Now no more
2760The juice of Egypt’s grape shall moist this lip.

Charmian and Iras begin to dress her.

2761Yare, yare, good Iras, quick. Methinks I hear
2762Antony call. I see him rouse himself
2763To praise my noble act. I hear him mock
2764The luck of Caesar, which the gods give men
2765To excuse their after wrath.—Husband, I come!
2766Now to that name my courage prove my title.
2767I am fire and air; my other elements
2768I give to baser life.—So, have you done?
2769Come then, and take the last warmth of my lips.
2770Farewell, kind Charmian.—Iras, long farewell.

She kisses them. Iras falls and dies.

2771Have I the aspic in my lips? Dost fall?
2772If thou and nature can so gently part,
2773The stroke of death is as a lover’s pinch,
2774Which hurts and is desired. Dost thou lie still?
2775If thus thou vanishest, thou tell’st the world
2776It is not worth leave-taking.

CHARMIAN

2777Dissolve, thick cloud, and rain, that I may say
2778The gods themselves do weep!

CLEOPATRA

The gods themselves do weep! This proves me base.
2779If she first meet the curlèd Antony,
2780He’ll make demand of her, and spend that kiss

2786Unpolicied!

2810A way there, a way for Caesar!

That you did fear is done. Bravest at the last,
2813She leveled at our purposes and, being royal,

FIRST GUARD

2818This Charmian lived but now; she stood and spake.
2819I found her trimming up the diadem
2820On her dead mistress; tremblingly she stood,
2821And on the sudden dropped.

CAESAR

And on the sudden dropped. O, noble weakness!
2822If they had swallowed poison, ’twould appear
2823By external swelling; but she looks like sleep,
2824As she would catch another Antony

DOLABELLA

In her strong toil of grace. Here on her breast
2826There is a vent of blood, and something blown.
2827The like is on her arm.

FIRST GUARD

2828This is an aspic’s trail, and these fig leaves
2829Have slime upon them, such as th’ aspic leaves
2830Upon the caves of Nile.

CAESAR

Upon the caves of Nile. Most probable
2831That so she died, for her physician tells me
2832She hath pursued conclusions infinite
2833Of easy ways to die. Take up her bed,
2834And bear her women from the monument.
2835She shall be buried by her Antony.
2836No grave upon the earth shall clip in it
2837A pair so famous. High events as these
2838Strike those that make them; and their story is
2839No less in pity than his glory which
2840Brought them to be lamented. Our army shall
2841In solemn show attend this funeral,
2842And then to Rome. Come, Dolabella, see
2843High order in this great solemnity.

They all exit, the Guards bearing the dead bodies.

Entran César, Agripa y Mecenas, con su ejército; César, leyendo una carta

CÉSAR

1801Dice que soy un niño, y me reprueba como si tuviera
1802poder para echarme de Egipto. A mi mensajero
1803lo ha mandado azotar, y a mí en persona me desafía:
1804“César contra Antonio”. Ese viejo ha de saber
1805que tengo otros planes para morir; mientras tanto
1806me río de sus amenazas.

MECENAS

me río de sus amenazas. Tenga César presente
1807que cuando un gran hombre se enfurece se sabe acorralado
1808y su caída inminente. No le deis respiro, y ahora
1809sacad provecho de su confusión. Nunca fue la ira
1810buen centinela de sí misma.

CÉSAR

buen centinela de sí misma. Sepan nuestros oficiales
1811que de librar mañana la última de muchas batallas
1812tenemos intención. En nuestras filas contamos
1813con soldados que solían servir a Marco Antonio
1814suficientes para prenderlo. Ved que así se haga,
1815y que haya fiestas para la tropa. Víveres nos sobran,
1816y se han merecido el gasto. ¡Pobre Antonio!

TODOS

1846No puedo despediros; como señor vuestro quedo
1847esposado a vuestro fiel servicio hasta la muerte.

ENOBARBO

1850¿Para qué queréis desconsolarnos? Mirad cómo lloran.

ANTONIO

1853¡Que la bruja se me lleve si esa fuera mi intención!
1854Crezca la gracia donde caen esas lágrimas, amigos generosos.
1855Doloroso en exceso es el sentido que dais a mis palabras.
